lawyer:
Moksudor Rahman with Akram Hossain Amin and Dr. AKM Ali, Advocates ----- For the Petitioner in Writ Petition No. 88 of 1995
ABM Nurul Islam with Farah Mahmuda and Alauddin Khalid, Advocates ----- For the Petitioner in Writ Petition No. 161 of 1995

parties:
Raufique (Md) Hossain ------ Petitioner 
[In Writ Petition 88 of 1995] 
Md. Alauddin Khalid   ------ Petitioner 
[In Writ Petition 161 of 1995] 
vs.
Speaker, Bangladesh Parliament and others ------ Respondents 
[In all the Writ Petitions]
full_judgment:
3. Both the writ petitions arise out of resignation of the seats of Parliament by 147 Members of the Parliament. But at the outset I must say that Writ Petition No. 88 of 1995 has been drafted haphazardly in an unusual manner and the events that led to file the petition are founded mostly on the news items published in the different national dailies of the country on different dates which are annexed to this petition in support of the statement of the petitioner. However, the narration of the episode, which led to the submission of the resignation letters and gave rise to these two petitions viz, Writ Petition Nos. 88 and 161 of 1995, in short, is that the election of the members of the 5th Parliament was held on 27.2.91 and after publication of the result in Gazette Notification the members elected took oath of their office. The respondents 3-5 were elected from respective constituencies. Respondent 3, Mrs. Sk. Hasina alias Sk. Hasina Wazed is the President of the Awami League and leader of the Opposition in the Parliament. Respondent 4 is the Acting Leader of the Jatiya Party in the Parliament while respondent No.5 is the leader of the Jamaat-e-Islami Party in the Parliament in Writ Petition No.88 of 1995. After the election the Parliament has been holding sessions regularly for legislative functions. But the respondents 3-5 along with the members of the Parliament belonging to their respective parties had been abstaining from attending the sessions of the Parliament from March 1, 1994 on the plea of non-acceptance of their demand by the Treasury Bench headed by the Prime Minister Begum Khaleda Zia for holding next general election of the members of the Parliament under a caretaker Government. That demand was made as they thought that no fair and free election could he held under the umbrella of the ruling party. It was further stated that not only the opposition members of the Parliament started boycott of the sessions of the Parliament but they also called hartals frequently to press home their demand and such boycott and hartals led one Mr. Anwar Hossain Khan to file Writ Petition No. 1001 of 1994 for a declaration, amongst others, that the unabated boycott by the opposition members was unconstitutional and void. The Constitutional Bench, however, on contest made the Rule absolute and declared, amongst others, the boycott and the demand for care-taker government void and unconstitutional with a further direction to the respondents 3-5 to attend the Parliament. It stated that demand for care-taker government was made following the result of by-election in the Magura-2 constituency held on 20.3.94 and the boycott of the Parliament created a serious political crisis and Sir Ninian Stephen, a Special Envoy of the Commonwealth Secretary General, came to Bangladesh to resolve the political deadlock He held dialogue between the competiting compass of political parties without any fruitful result and he left Bangladesh on 21.11.94. The petitioner further states that even after the failure of Sir Stephen attempts were made to continue the dialogue to solve the problem in different ways and the people were in serious tension every moment awaiting in anxious expectation for peaceful solution of the political impasse. But all were futile attempts and the opposition members of the Parliament submitted their resignation letters to the respondent 1 on 28.12.94 at 9-13 PM. The petitioner also states what happened on the eve of the submission of the resignation letters on that fateful night quoting from the news published in his petition. He states that on 28.12.94 at 7-15 PM Mrs. Sheikh Hasina along with other leaders went to the Chamber of the respondent 1 to submit resignation letters. But the respondent 1 led them to his "call-on-room" for another round of talks. After several rounds of telephonic talk a Government team of three members Prof Budruddoza Chowdhury, Mr. Abdus Salam Talukder and Mr. Oli Ahmed, came to the Parliament reportedly to sign an agreement with the opposition parties. But as the talk with the opposition leaders broke down the leaders of the ruling party left the Parliament around 9-10 PM and the Whips of the respective opposition parties submitted the identically worded resignation letters to the respondent 1 Mr. Sk. Rajjak Ali, the Speaker. The reason for failure of the talk was reported to be, according to the opposition parties, that ruling party introduced some new condition while the negotiators of the ruling party alleged that the opposition parties were going back from the commitment. It is stated that for accepting the demand of the opposition that the Prime Minister should not continue in office after the expiry of the term and the President was to conduct election the ruling party demanded a guarantee from the opposition parties that they would desist from calling any hartal or siege programme for the rest of the current term of the 5th Parliament. Imposition of this condition was considered by the opposition leaders an infringement of their fundamental political right of mass agitation and demonstration and for imposition of such conditions the last 'ditch-effort' fizzled out and 147 members of the Parliament tendered their resignation letters to the respondent 1. Mr. Azizur Rahman, Awami League Whip, submitted 93 resignation letters of the Members of the Parliament belonging to Awami League, Mr. Monirul Hoque Chowdhury submitted 34 resignation letters of the Members of the Parliament of the Jatiya Party while Mr. Latifur Rahman submitted 19 resignation letters of the Members of Parliament of the Jamaat-e-Islami and Mr. Salahuddin Kader Chowdhury, the leader of the Nationalist Democratic Party submitted his resignation letter peronally to the respondent 1. The resignation letters were worded in identical words stating that they were compelled to resign in the greater interest of the country as the Bangladesh Nationalist Party Government had rendered Parliament ineffective and each resignation letter contained the signature of the individual Member of the Parliament. After the resignation letters were submitted, it is stated by the petitioner, quoting from the newspaper, that as a part of the effort to save the nation from confrontation the opposition parties abstained from submitting the resignation letters even after the deadline mentioned and shifted from their original position but the Government foiled the sincere effort. The petitioner also quotes the statement of Moulana Matiur Rahman Nizami published in the newspaper saying that resignation letters were an expression of "........................no confidence in the 5th Parliament and the BNP Government, and both now lost their legitimacy." The petitioner again quoted a portion of the news published in the 'Daily Star' on 29.12.94. The summary of which is that former Minister and Jatiya Party Member of the Parliament Maj. Genl.(Retd) Mahmudul Hasan revolted against party decision on resignation from Parliament and joined Bangladesh Nationalist Party and Mr. Mizanur Rahman Chowdhury, acting Chairman of Jatiya Party, expressed his surprise at the joining of Mr. Mahmudul Hasan to Bangladesh Nationalist Party. He said that all Members of the Parliament of Jatiya Party had submitted their resignation letters to him a few days ago on the decision of the Presidium of the Jatiya Party decision to resign. He further quoted the news that the Awami League Chief Sk. Hasina announced at a huge rally that the Prime Minister should resign following the announcement of Election Schedule and the President would dissolve Parliament and form an interim government with either a serving or a retired judge of Appellate Division of the Supreme Court or a non-partisan personality as the Prime Minister with an Advisory Council and the members of the Council will be the nominee of the ruling party and the opposition parties. The Jatiya Party and the Jamaat-e-Islami also in their respective rallies announced that the interim government would be dissolved with the appointment of the new Prime Minister after the general election and the new frame-work would be ratified by the next elected Parliament. Mrs. Sk. Hasina also announced that after their resignation they would launch movement for the single demand for resignation of the Government of Begum Khaleda Zia to ensure free and fair election under non-party care-taker administration. He also quotes the news appeard in 'Daily Star' on 30.12.94, 31.12.84 and 5.1.1995 and 6.1.1995 which published the news that Prima Minister told at a public meeting opposition should revise the decision while Mrs. Hasina asked the Government to resign and to hold election as per opposition formula. It also reported that the Prime Minister had said that the country was to be run as per Constitution, and the Bangladesh Nationalist Party would not accept the Advisory Council and the opposition had said that the election was the only solution. It further reported that Mrs. Sk. Hasina wanted dissolution of the Jatiya Sangsad and hold a fresh election and Awami League urged the Government to return to the path of peace. But the Jatiya Party had said that there was no possibility of compromise but a discussion regarding when and how the government would resign and hold general election under the care-taker administration might be held. The petitioner also quoted the news appeared on 6.1.95 to the effect "efforts are still on for amicable solution to the persisting political impasse to avoid an apprehended confrontation between the opposing political camps following the en masse resignation of 147 opposition law-makers". The petitioner states further that resignation was piloted by the leaders of their respective parties including respondents 3-5 and the resigning members did not exercise their power of resignation in good faith under Article 67(2) which enables an individual member to resign for unavoidable reason and Article 67(2) does not contemplate en masse resignation under the pressure of the political parties. The petitioner further states that last parliamentary election held on 27.2.1991 was not held under a care-taker government as claimed by the opposition political parties but it was held under an interim Government when the former Chief Justice Mr. Justice Shahabuddin Ahmed performed the functions of the President being appointed the Vice President by the outgoing President HM Ershad to enable him to transfer power within the existing Constitutional scheme, the Presidential System of Government, which had nothing to do with holding an election of Members of the parliament and 12th Amendment of the Constitution has brought about a change in the method of transfer of power to the successor government through parliamentary election but the political leaders misled the people that the present government has come to power through election held under a care-taker Government. He states that the Government of Justice Shahabuddin Ahmed had no role in holding election except to place some necessary staff at the disposal of the Election Commission. He further states that members of the Parliament had taken oath to discharge their duties faithfully according to law but they have violated the oath by resigning seats. In the supplementary affidavit the petitioner states the 'Daily Dinkal' in its issue dated 3.1.1995 reported, that doubt had arisen in the mind of the Members of the Parliament belonging to the opposition parties that the resignation letters were not separately written. (Annexure-C to the supplementary affidavit is the copy of the daily Dinkal dated 3.1.1995). 

 7. The respondent 3 in her affidavit-in- opposition raised a preliminary objection to the maintainability of this writ petition on the ground that the petitioner has no locus standi to file the writ petition as he is not "a person aggrieved" within the meaning of Article 102 (2) of the Constitution and she including respondents 4, 5 are not "persons" within the meaning of Article 102(2)(a)(ii) of the Constitution inasmuch as they are not performing function in connection with the affairs of the Republic and in no way related to any statutory body and that the petition is premature, as according to the statement of the petitioner, the Speaker is yet to give decision on the submission of the resignation letters; The learned counsel for Respondent 3 also took the stand that this court is debarred from exercising its power as vested under Article 102 of the Constitution in view of Article 78(2) of the Constitution inasmuch as resignation relates to functioning of the Parliament, the powers and privileges of the members of the Parliament and is not amenable to judicial review by this court. There is no cause of action for this petition; the issues involved in this petition are of political nature and are beyond the ambit of Article 102 of the Constitution. As the petition is malafide and suffers from inordinate delay, filed after 9 months from the date all the opposition political parties launched movement for restoration of voting rights of the citizen by calling hartals, procession and holding meetings in order to ensure democracy, by holding free and fair election, this court should not exercise its discretion conferred under Article 102 of the Constitution; the petition suffers from defect of parties; it raises disputed question of facts regarding coercion in obtaining resignation letters from the resigning members of Parliament; the respondent 3 denies the truth of the statement of the petition that the 147 members of the Parliament resign their seat malafide to create political crisis and states that as the members acted in accordance with their constitutional right as envisaged under Article 67(2) of the Constitution this court cannot interfere with exercise of such constitutional right; the petitioner has failed to make out a case that his legal right is injured by reasons of resignation and that Article 67 (2) read with Rules 177 and 178 of the Rules of Procedure of Parliament of the People's Republic of Bangladesh (hereinafter shall be called the Rules) do not make any distinction between resignation and en-masse resignation. The respondent 3 also denied the allegations of the petitioner that the respondents are not performing their duties. And she, on the other hand, asserts that movement for care-taker government is a political movement for ensuring voting right of the people which is essential for democracy. She states that the petition founded on the statements made in paras 8-10 are based on the newspaper cutting relating to political issues cannot be considered by this court as news published in newspaper are not simpliciter admissible evidence; she asserts that each Member of the Parliament of the opposition parties specially of the Awami League had tendered their resignation letters separately and voluntarily in writing without any coercion in obedience to the decision of their respective parties and denies the statement that the resignation letters were submitted under coercion. She further states that none of the resigning members ever denied the fact that they voluntarily resigned on 28.12.94. She also asserts that the Election Commission has been rendered useless as it solely depends on the Government and the Bangladesh Nationalist Party government in by-election held in Mirpur and Magura proved that they are interested in corrupt practices. With reference to the statement of paragraph 16 of the writ petition respondent 3 states that all the opposition political parties represent 69% of the electorate and the Bangladesh Nationalist Party is afraid of holding election under care-taker government for losing in the election and it wants to remain in power practising fraud upon the electorate and the plea of amendment of the Constitution for care-taker government is fraudulent excuse to stay in power. It is further stated that as the present Government is the creation of care-taker Government it should have accepted the demand of the opposition parties but the government is not accepting as it wants to indulge in corrupt practices in election which it had adopted in by-election of Magura. She also denied the statements that by resignation the Members of the Parliament have faulted their oath. 

 8. Respondent 4 in his Affidavit-in-opposition states that the petitioner has no locus standi and the writ petition has been filed for political purpose as public interest litigation; the petition is also premature as the resignation letters are pending with the respondent 1 who has not yet given his decision thereon and he denies the statement of the petition that the leaders of the respective political party piloted resignation and that the members of the parliament had not exercised their power in good faith and that they were compelled to resign. He states that the resignation letters were submitted bonafide, voluntarily and those are genuine as they resigned after it was made clear to ruling party by announcing in the meeting of the respective parties held on 5.12.1994 that each member expressed his desire to resign voluntarily if the demand for amendment of the Constitution for care-taker Government is not accepted by the Government as similar decision was announced on 6.12.94 in the public meeting of the Jatiya Party that the members of the Parliament would resign on 28.12.94 if the demand was not accepted by 27.12.94. Respondent 4 denies the statement of the petitioner that submission of resignation is fraud upon the Constitution and the law. The respondent 4 like respondent 3 states that the present government came to power through a fair and free election held under a non-partisan government headed by the Chief Justice Mr. Justice Shahabuddin Ahmed. It is further stated that on 28.12.94 each member signed the resignation letter individually and when went to the Parliament accompanied by their leaders to submit resignation letters they were informed about the willingness of the government to come to an amicable settlement submission of resignation letters was withheld for two hours. Prof. Badruddoza Chowdhury. Mr. Oli Ahmed and Mr. Abdus Salam Talukder, however, arrived at 9-00 PM and informed that government accepted the demand of the opposition and the Prime Minister had agreed to resign 30 days prior to the national election. Respondent 4 also states that the Speaker was told that resigning members were present and should be available when called by the Speaker, In the further affidavit-in-opposition he stated that the petitioner is a political worker who filed the petition malafide at the instance of an influential faction of ruling party and the statements based on inaccurate news items cannot be relied upon. 

 9. Respondent 5 similarly states that the petitioner has no locus standi and the writ petition is outside the scope of judicial review under Article 102 of the Constitution. He also echoed the voice of respondent 3 that the opposition parties represent 69% electorate of the country and the demand for holding election under a care-taker government is a democratic demand. It is further stated that mere existence of Election Commission is not the guarantee for holding fair and free election and in 1991 the election held under the care- taker government was the free and fair one. He denies the statement that in 1991 parliamentary election was not held under care-taker government. He further denies that resignation by 147 Members of the Parliament is threat to the Constitutional deadlock and to peace and harmony in the society. He also states that news reports arc nothing but mere surmises and conjectures. 

 10. Respondents 1 and 2 state that petition is premature and not maintainable as it was filed when the resignation letters were awaiting the decision of the respondent 1. With reference to the statements made in paras 12 and 13 of the petition it states that on 28.12.94 at about 9-00 PM respondent 1 received 3 folders said to contain resignation letters submitted by the 147 Members of Parliament-one was filed by Mr. Matiur Rahman the other by Mr. Mizanur Rahman Chowdhury and another by Moulana Nizami. The respondent 1 immediately after receipt of the folders announced that those required scrutiny as per Article 67(2) and Rule 177 of the Rules of Procedure of the Parliament of the People's Republic of Bangladesh and requested the members of the Parliament who resigned their seats to appear before him in his office and when he called the name of some Members of the Jamaat-e-Islami he found nobody of the three political parties present except Mr. Salahuddin Kader Chowdhury of the National Democratic Party (NDP). Thereafter respondent 1 told the waiting journalists about receipt of the folders and of the absence of the members. He also told that he required time necessary to examine the resignation letters contained in the folders as per Constitution. These statements are also made on the basis of the news published on 29.12.94 (Annexures 1, 2, 3, 4& 5). It is further stated that on scrutiny it was found that signature on the resignation letters of two members of the Parliament belonging to the Awami League did not tally with their specimen signatures kept in the Parliament Secretariat and these letters did not bear any date. It is stated that the discrepancy required verification as to the genuineness of the resignation. It is stated further that Mr. Akhtaruzzaman MP was absconding and Mr. Mustafizur Rahman, MP by a letter informed on 28.12.94 that he did not submit any resignation letter. Maj. General (Retd.) Mahmudul Hasan of Jatiya Party by a letter dated 28.12.94 also informed that he had decided not to resign although his resignation letter was found in the folder submitted by Mizanur Rahman Chowdhury. It is also stated that some of the letters found in the folder were antedated showing the dates as 8.11.94 and 9.11.94. On 30.12.94 respondent 1 fell sick and was in Suhrawardy Hospital till 4.1.95. on his release, in spite of the advice of the Doctor to take rest, he resumed duty on 6.1.95 because of the urgency of the matter. It is stated that on verification respondent 1 found that in almost in all the resignation letters reason assigned was the failure of the ruling party to amend the Constitution for holding election under a neutral government and since the matter involves intricate constitutional and legal aspect he needed more time for scrutiny, etc. and he issued press release on 12.1.95 (Annexures 6-9). He denies the statement of the respondents 3-5 that Parliamentary election held on 27.2.91 was held under a care-taker government and states that it was held under the interim Government. It is further stated that neither the Constitution nor the Rule prescribes any time limit for scrutiny of the resignation letters and failure to complete verification and examination of resignation letters within two weeks is no failure to discharge his function calling for interference by this Court. It is further stated the even after submission of resignation letters negotiations between the ruling party and the opposition party continued to resolve the crisis which facts were published in the national daily as press briefing and the statements made by the leaders. 

 11. Respondent 7 also filed an Affidavit-in-opposition stating that although no Rule is issued against it but it appears as is impleaded as Respondent in the petition and states that filing of this Affidavit-in-opposition is necessitated for controverting and for denial of the allegation made against it by the Respondents 3-5 in the" Affidavit-in-opposition. Although it is stated that the extent of the authority of the Speaker to examine and decide as to the genuineness and voluntary nature of the resignation letters involves questions of interpretation of the Constitution and law, the privilege and the jurisdiction of the High Court Division to entertain writ petition. But also states that the petitioner is not a "person aggrieved" and, as such, cannot invoke writ jurisdiction and the petition is not maintainable. It terms the statement of the respondents 3-5 that if the Prime Minister remains in power she will influence the process of election of the Member of the Parliament and the voters of our country cannot exercise their franchise according to their free will as baseless and not correct. It further states that there is no provision for holding election under care-taker Government in the Constitution and such demand is contrary to the Constitution and submission of resignation by 147 members of the parliament created critical situation. It further states that as no Rule is issued on the respondent 7 the allegation made by respondents 3-5 in their affidavit- in-opposition against the respondent 7 are not justified and it denies the allegation made against the government. It further states that the statement of the respondents 3-5 that movement for care-taker government is constitutional and for ensuring the democratic right to the people is not correct and also denies the statements of respondent 3-5 that the Election Commission is totally and solely dependent on the Government. It further states that as the Bangladesh Nationalist Party is not impleaded as party in the writ petition it is unfair and unwarranted to make allegations against the said party which should go unconsidered by this court as these are motivated and are of political nature. It further states that allegations against Members who are not parties in this petition are ill founded and are denied. It further states that the statement of the respondent Nos. 3-5 that any democratic government would have responded to the demand of the respondents 3-5 is not correct inasmuch as the government is to function in accordance with the provision of law and it has no obligation to accept unconstitutional political demand. It further denies the truth of the statement of the respondents 3-5 that the Returning Officers being civil servants cannot work independently. It is stated that the allegation that there is intolerance, inaptness, insolence, arrogance, obstinacy and lack of experience and apprehension on the part of the government are irrelevant and unwarranted for the purpose of this Rule as those are political issues and ought not to have been raised in the writ petition. It further denies the statement made by respondents 3-5 that the present government has lost its popularity and legitimacy. It asserts that the statement made in paragraphs 43-45 of the Affidavit-in-opposition requires strict proof thereof by the makers of the statement. The statement that the writ petition was filed with the intent to enable the government to stay in power for long as possible has also been denied. It asserts that the government and the Parliament are functioning according to the Constitution. It further denies the truth of the allegations that if the Prime Minister remains in power at the time of ejection she will try to influence the process of the election and states that the allegation is malicious and it is not correct to say on the part of the respondents 3-5 that Prime Minister did not take part in the debates nor made any statement on the issues mentioned in para 26(iv) of the Affidavit-in-opposition of respondent 4 and that the Prime Minister absented from the proceeding of the Parliament for 3 years or she failed to take part in any of the 4 budget proceedings. The allegation made against the Ministers who are not parties are unfair and unwarranted and denies the statement that a Member of the Cabinet was compelled to resign on the issue of Care-taker Government. 

 19. Mr. Moksudur Rahman in reply to the preliminary objection raised by the respondents vehemently argued that petitioner, a citizen of Bangladesh and a member of the Dhaka District Bar, like other citizens who are politically conscious has got locus standi to file the writ petition before this court. He continues to argue that the resignation has affected the petitioner because the petitioner is vitally interested in orderly running of the Government and the election of the members of the Parliament according to the Constitution but resignation has posed an imminent danger to a Constitutional deadlock and threat to the peace and harmony in the society and holding of frequent hartals by the members of the opposition parties has affected the democratic process. On the contention of prematurity of this writ petition he submits that cause of action has not arisen as the matter of resignation of 147 is pending with the respondent 1 as contended by the respondent is not correct and submits that it has arisen from March 1, 1994 and cause of action is a recurring one continued till submission of resignation letters. He further submits on the merit of the case that the petition is made bonafide and shall not defeat on the ground of malafide as contended by the respondents. 

 He also argued that Article 67(2) does not conceive of en masse resignation and such resignation is malafide and constitutes fraud upon the Constitution and by such resignation the Parliament has been crippled and the democracy is halted. He further referred us to the preamble of the Constitution and Articles 8, 11, 21 and 75(i)(b) to contend that the resignation of the present nature is not only opposed to Article 67(2) but it is also opposed to the concept of the democracy as enshrined in the preamble, Articles 8 and 11 of the Constitution. Relying on Article 21 he submits that it is the duty of every citizen to observe the Constitution and the laws but the 147 members of Parliament by resigning en massee have violated the provision of Articles 8, 11 and 21. It is pertinent to say that those Articles fall under Part-II of the Constitution and relate to the Parliament Principles of State Policy. He further contends that the resignation letters were procured for collateral purpose to achieve the common goal for holding general election under a care-taker Government which is not contemplated under the Constitution. 

 The decision of Rajnarayan Singh vs. Atmaram Convind, 1954 (All) 319 may be referred to. In that decision their Lordships explained what is parliamentary privilege. It is held that Parliamentary privilege of the House of Commons of United Kingdom means that sum of the fundamental rights of the House and of its individual members as against the prerogative of the Crown, the authority of the ordinary Courts of law and the special rights of the House of Lords. The aforesaid observation is in the line of the observation made in the case of Bradlaugh vs. Grosett as referred to earlier in our judgment. In the case of Harendra Nalh Barua vs. Bev Kania Barua, 1958 Assam 160 a similar question fell for determination by their Lordships regarding the rights and privileges of the House of Parliament and the House of State Legislature. Sarjoo Prosad, CJ after reviewing the constitutional provision of Britain, Australia in this regard observed: 

 From Article 102(2) (a) it is seen that petitioner who wants a direction upon persons performing any functions in connection with the affairs of the Republic from this Division in the nature as contained in Article 102(2) (a) (i) or a declaration that an act or proceeding taken by such persons has been done or taken under Article 102(2) (a) (ii) without lawful authority and is of no legal effect must satisfy the court that he is a "person aggrieved". Now, I revert back to the cases relied upon by Mr. Nabi. He cited the following decisions:- The cases Bar Council vs. MV Dabholkar, 1975 (SC) 2095, DC Nakara and others vs. Union of India, 1983 (SC) 103, Dr. DC Wadhwa and others vs. State of Bihar and others, 1987 (SC) 579, Bangladesh Sangbad Patra Parishad (BSP) vs. Government of the People's Republic of Bangladesh, 43 DLR (AD) 126. In the case of Bar Council Supreme Court of India, while expressing its opinion on the meaning of the words a "person aggrieved" held that "one of the meanings is that a person will be held to be aggrieved by a decision if that decision is materially adverse to him. Normally, one is required to establish that one has been denied or deprived of something to which one is legally entitled in order to make one a "person aggrieved". It further held "The test is whether the words a "person aggrieved" include a person who has genuine grievance because an order has been made prejudicially affects his interests". DS Nakara and others vs. Union India AIR 1983 (SC) 130 is a case of public interest litigation. The petitioner No.3, in that case, a registered Society under Society Registration Act of 1860, was a non-political, non-profit and voluntary organization. Its members consist of public spirited citizens seeking to espouse cause of legitimate public interest. The Society received a large number of representations from old pensioners who were individually unable to undertake the journey through "labyrinths" of legal judicial process, costly and protected......................... "The case of Dr. DC Wadhwa and others vs. State of Bihar and others AIR 1987 (SC) 579, is also a Social Action Litigation (SAL). In that case the petitioner was a professional economist and has spent a number of years in studying the constitutional functioning of Indian politics and was deeply interested in the preservation and promotion of constitutional functioning of the administration in his country. In that case the petition challenged the power of the Governor of Bihar under Article 213 of the Indian Constitution to repromulgate ordinances from time to time without getting them replaced by Acts of the Legislature under Article 32 of the Constitution of India. The Supreme Court held that the petitioner because of his substantial contribution through research in the field to ensure proper implementation of the Constitutional Provision had locus standi to challenge the practice of the Bihar State to promulgate and repromulgate the Ordinance from time to time without enacting them into Acts of the legislature for vindication of public interests although it held that a petition is not entitled to challenge an Ordinance merely as a member of public unless some legal right or interest of his is violated or threatened by such Ordinance. 

 24. Mr. Nabi also argued that the writ petition is premature as the resignation letters submitted to the Speaker becomes effective when the Speaker determines its genuineness and submits that as the Speaker has not taken any step the writ petition is premature. This contention of Mr. Nabi is in contradiction of his submission that the resignation takes it effect as soon as the Speaker receives the same. However, in support of his contention of prematurity of the writ petition he cites the decision in the cases of Surat Singh Yadav vs. Sudama Prasad Goswami and another, 1965 All 536, Jagat Singh and ors. vs. State of Uttar Prodesh and another, 1962 (All) 606, Mohammad Mohideen vs. State Wakf Board and others, 1963 Mad 132, and the case of Universal Imports Agency & another vs. Chief Controller of Imports and Exports and others, 1961 (SC) 41. In Sural Singh Yadav, Sree Sudama Prasad Goswami, the opposite Party 1, was elected a member of the Bidhan Sabha of Uttar Pradesh on the Congress ticket. He resigned his seat in the Vidhan Sabha on the ground of arrest of one Raghu Nath Singh in connection with a dacoity case. Raghu Nath was a member of Janshangha party. Sudama Prosad announced in a public meeting held on 7.10.1963 that he had resigned his seat and sent his resignation letter to the Speaker of the Vidhan Sabha. But it was found that the resignation letter was sent to the President of All India Congress Committee and copy of the same to the President of the UP Congress Committee and to the President of the District Congress Committee. It was not sent to the Speaker. Later on the Speaker received resignation letter and read out in the Vidhan Sabha pointing out that the resignation letter was not in proper form as it did not mention from which date the member was resigning nor did it mention the time of the resignation letter. Consequently the Speaker declared that he would take action under Rule 268 of the Rules of Procedure and Conduct of Business of UP Legislative Assembly, 1958, to satisfy himself regarding the genuineness and voluntary nature of the resignation letter before giving his decision. The writ petition was filed before the Speaker had taken decision in this regard. In Jagat Singh it was held, on the facts of that case, that although the petitioner was able to show that there was a potential threat to the invasion of his right to obtain an adequate compensation under S.299 of the Government of India Act, 1935 the petition was liable to be dismissed on the ground of being premature as potential threat cannot be the cause of action for a petition under Article 226 of the Indian Constitution. In Mohammad Mohideen it was held that as there was dispute as to the propriety of the removal of the petitioner from mutawalliship it was for the Board who had a prima facie jurisdiction to go into the question of merit and as the allegation was before the Board it was held that for purpose of deciding the allegations the Wakf Board had jurisdiction and accordingly, the petition under Article 226 of the Constitution was held to be premature. The case of Universal Import Agency (AIR 1961 (SC) 41) is on different facts.  28. Mr. Moksudur Rahman stoutly made an attempt to repel the contention of the Respondent on the maintainability of the writ petition under Article 102 of our Constitution. He contends that the petitioner has got locus standi and heavily relied on the decision in the case of Kazi Moklesor Rahman vs. Bangladesh and others, 26 DLR (AD) 44. The fact of this case was that the petitioner filed a writ petition under Article 102(2)(a)(ii) of the Constitution for a declaration that agreement between the Governments of the People's Republic of Bangladesh and the Republic of India signed on 16.5.1974 by the Prime Ministers of the two countries involving cessation of Bangladesh territory was without lawful authority and of no legal effect. The petition relates to Barubari Union No. 12 and the adjacent enclaves which were under the administrative control of Indian state. The writ petition was summarily dismissed by the High Court Division holding that the petitioner had no locus standi. The petitioner admittedly was not a resident of any part of the territories in the aforesaid agreement which is called the Delhi treaty. The respondent contended before the Supreme Court that the petitioner as such had no interest which could be affected by the treaty and as such was not" a person aggrieved" within the meaning of Article 102(2) of the Constitution. The Supreme Court referred a large number of decisions of India, Pakistan, Australia, US and of English jurisdiction on this point. In delivering the judgment of the report Sayem, CJ observed "It appears to us that the question of locus standi does not involve the court's jurisdiction to hear a person but of the competency of the person to claim a hearing so that the question is one of discretion which the court exercises upon due consideration of the facts and circumstances of each case. The appellant has complained that he is under an impending threat of deprivation of his fundamental rights under Article 36 of the Constitution and his right of franchise. Because of this as well as of the exceptional and extraordinary Constitutional issue raised in this case involving consideration of an international agreement between this country and the friendly Republic of India, we decided to hear the appellant". But the Supreme Court having taken the view that the treaty making power though falls within the ambit of the executive power under Article 55(2) of the Constitution the present treaty involving cessation of territory can only be concluded by amendment of Article 2(a) by taking recourse to Article 142 of the Constitution. It was further held that as no such amendment was made the writ petition before the High Court was premature and upon such finding the appeal was dismissed. Mr. Moksudur Rahman also referred to the decision in the case of Anwar Hussain vs Bangladesh, popularly known as Constitution 8th Amendment case, 41 DLR (AD) 165 and referred to paragraph Nos. 61 and 62 of the judgment. The facts of that case, in short, are that by Martial Law Proclamation Order No. 11 of 1982 High Court Division of the Supreme Court was bifurcated by establishing seven permanent Benches at Dhaka, Rangpur, Jessore, Comilla, Chittagong, Sylhet and Barisal. Lawyers started movement against such fragmentation of the High Court Division. When the Constitution was revived the permanent Benches outside the capital were treated as Sessions of the High Court Division outside the capital. Lawyers contended that this was unconstitutional and there was stalemate. On 9.6.1988 Article 100 of the Constitution was amended setting up six permanent Benches at Rangpur, Jessore, Barisal, Chittagong, Com ilia and Sylhet and as the President was authorized to fix the territorial jurisdiction of the High Court Division in the permanent seat he issued notifications conferring upon the High Court Division and the permanent Benches mutually exclusive jurisdiction. The Chief Justice also framed rules importing the concept of "cases arising out of an area" and providing for transfer of pending proceedings from High Court Division to permanent Benches. Writ petitions were filed challenging the amendment of Article 100 of the Constitution of the People's Republic of Bangladesh and the Rules on various grounds, the most important ground was that High Court Division of the Supreme Court with plenary judicial power over the Republic is a basic structure of the Constitution which cannot be altered or damaged and the amendment is void having rendered the High Court Division with plenary judicial power over the entire Republic non-existent. The High Court Division refused to issue a Rule holding that the impugned amendment has not destroyed or damaged the basic stricture of the Constitution as the High Court Division has full powers and jurisdiction subject to Article 100(5) of the Constitution. On appeal to the Appellate Division by a majority of 3: 1 Appellate Division held that amendment of Article 100 was void. As in that case the writ petition challenged on the authority of the President for amendment of Article 100 of the Constitution and the decision was given on the power of the President to promulgate Ordinance to set up permanent Benches of the Supreme Court and as in the instant writ petition no such question on the amending power of the Parliament is raised for our determination this case of Anwar Hossain is of no assistance to him. He further cited the case of Pakistan vs. Ahmed Sayeed Kirmani, PLD 1958 (SC) 397, the case of SP Gupta and others vs. M Tarkunde and others AIR 1982 (SC) 149, (para 17-23), the case of Gali Kondaiah vs Gali Ankamma AIR 1988 (AP) 69. In Sayeed Kirmani "Mr. Ahmad Sayeed Kirmani, presumably a member of the Opposition, approached the High Court of West Pakistan for a writ of quo-warranto, mandamus, or any other appropriate writ, order or direction, declaring the election of the Speaker of the 20th May, 1956 to be null and void, directing Choudhri Fazal Elahi to prove his lawful authority to function as Speaker and directing Choudhir Fazal Elahi and the Secretary of the West Pakistan Legislative Assembly to enable Mir Muhammad Bakash Talpur and Mr. Varyani " to cast their votes according to their free will for the lawful election of the Speaker of the Assembly". The fact of this case is quite distinguishable from that facts of the case before us. The petitioner as a member of the West Pakistan Assembly had substantial interest in the matter of election of the Speaker and to see that his right to elect Speaker is not deprived of by any illegal decision of the Chairman who conducted the election. But before us the petitioner is not a member of the Parliament and his interest is not of the nature of the petitioner of writ petition before the West Pakistan High Court. Thus, this case does not help Mr. Moksudur Rahman. The case of SP Gupta is a case on public interest light and the principle laid down therein was enunciated relating to standing of a petitioner who brings an action before the Court to vindicate the right of socially disadvantaged group of people. That is not so here as the petitioner does not seek declaration for vindicating the right of the people, rather he moves this court in the writ jurisdiction to vindicate his own right. Thus, this case also does not help the petitioner to establish locus standi. The case of Goli Kondaiah has no relevance as it is cited to argue on defect of parties. As this Rule is discharged on the ground of maintainability this case does not require consideration. 

 30. The observation made in the decision of Indian jurisdiction were on the cases on either public interest litigation or on cases on social action litigations. The case before us is a litigation not of social action litigation or of public interest litigation as admitted by the petitioner in this case. Article 102 of our Constitution because of the expression a "person aggrieved" and expression "enforcement of any fundamental rights conferred by Part III of this Constitution" has narrowed down the scope of this writ jurisdiction unlike that of India under Article 226 in which the fathers of the constitution in their attempt to meet the social economic condition and for enforcement of such right widened the jurisdiction consciously. The decisions of Indian jurisdiction altogether are founded on different view on the finding of locus standi on the facts of each case based on the rights with reference to Article 226 of the Constitution of India which is differently worded other than fundamental rights as contemplated in Article 102 but it helps us indirectly to hold that unless the petitioner satisfied this Court about infringement of any constitutional rights or rights accrued under any Act of the Parliament no action as has been brought before us can stand. As I have examined several decisions cited at the Bar of the Indian jurisdiction I think that those are on the language employed in the Indian Constitution which is much wider in scope to apply high prerogative writs by the Supreme Court under Article 32 and by the respective High Courts of India under Article 226. But in view of the provision and the language used in Article 102 of our Constitution I must go by the pronouncements of this Division and Appellate Division of the Supreme Court of Bangladesh. The most important decision seems to me is the decision in the case of Bangladesh Sangbadpatra Parishad vs. Government of the People's Republic of Bangladesh in 43 DLR (AD) 126 wherein it has been held that "Therefore the decisions of the Indian jurisdiction on public interest litigation are hardly apt to our situation. We must confine ourselves to asking whether the petitioner is a "person aggrieved", a phrase which has received a meaning and a dimension over the years". In the light of the aforesaid observation made in the cases just referred to by me and the expression "aggrieved party" which finds place in Article 102(2)(a) of the Constitution of Bangladesh I am of the opinion that in order to invoke writ jurisdiction of this Court under Article 102(2)(a) of the Constitution of the People's Republic of Bangladesh in a writ of certiorari the petitioner must establish that by act done either his constitutional right or any legal right has been invaded and he has a direct and substantial interest in the matter. Because of en masse resignation it cannot be held that the petitioner is a "person aggrieved" within the meaning of Article 102(2) (a) as in the present case by such resignation no direct and substantial Constitutional or legal right of the petitioner has been infringed or he has been deprived of his right of franchise as contended by Mr. Moksudur Rahman nor resignation has acted as an imminent danger to any of constitutional or legal rights of the petitioner.

Mr. Asrarul Hossain, the learned counsel appearing for the respondents 1 and 2, on the other hand, seriously contends that there being no provision to submit resignation letters to the Election Commission and as under clause (2) of Article 67 of the Constitution resignation letters are to be submitted to the Speaker it clearly indicates that the Speaker has got to do something with regard to submission of the resignation letters which is implicit under Article 67. He further submits that Article 67 had 2 parts. If conditions enumerated under clause (1) occur the vacation of seat of a member of the Parliament is automatic. But under clause (2) of Article 67 there is no automatic vacation of seat. Pointing out to the difference between two clauses of Article 67 the learned counsel submits that because of this different constitutional consequence the respondent 1 requires time to examine the resignation letters. He submits that this view finds force in proviso to clause (1) of Rule 177 and clause (2) of Rule 178 as the same has the force of law, the Rules being framed under the authority of Article 76(1) of the Constitution. Therefore, Mr. Hossain submits that the contention of the petitioner that once a resignation always a resignation and so the resignation letters submitted to the respondent 1 takes automatic effect as contended by Mr. Nurul Islam cannot be accepted. Mr. Asrarul Hossain secondly, submits that the Court should not have hastened to issue this Rule because the petition is premature and the matter rests with the Speaker. Mr. Hossain argued also referring to Rule 316 that the matter of submission of resignation letters arise in connection with the business of the House and the decision of the Speaker is final. He puts great stress that as the resignation letters arise in connection with the business of the House this Court has got no jurisdiction to issue the Rule. I am unable to accept the contention of the learned counsel of the respondents 1 and 2. My reading of the Article 67(2) and Rule 316 is contrary to what he says. In the Writ Petition No.88 of 1995 I have addressed myself on the jurisdiction of this Court on submission of the resignation letters. I, therefore, do not want to give a repeated view of mine in this regard with a view to avoid lengthening the judgment any further. But just I read a few pages from AK Brohi's book "Fundamental Law of Pakistan" appearing at paragraph 77. The learned author speaks as, "The business of the legislature thus falls into three broad categories, legislative, financial and critical; it has to pass laws, to vote supplies and keep the conduct of Government under the searchlight of public criticism. "Therefore, the contention of Mr. Hossain based on Rule 316 that the Court has no jurisdiction to issue Rule as it has done in the present case has got no legal stand in view of the aforesaid expression which just I have quoted in my judgment as submission or resignation although is in connection with the business of Parliament but submission to the Speaker simpliciter, until the Speaker brings it to the notice of the House as mandated by Rule 178(3), cannot be said "business of the House" on the interpretation of Rule 316 which Mr. Hossain wants us to give. Thus, I do not find force in the contention of Mr. Asrarul Hossain based on Rule 316. Now, I proceed to examine the standing of this petitioner. The petitioner is an Advocate of this Court and is a conscious citizen and he has filed the Writ Petition No. 161 of 1995 to vindicate the democratic right of the people for a direction on respondent 1 for the purpose which I have already stated. On the statements made in the petition, the affidavit-in-opposition and the reply to the affidavit-in-opposition it is seen that the petitioner does not claim that he has brought this action in the nature of public interest litigation nor social action litigation. Therefore, remedy sought to have arisen is on his independent right, either constitutional or legal. He founded his petition on the averments that he has right like the conscious citizen of the country that the respondent 1 should perform his function as contemplated under the Constitution and Rule and as withholding of his such function is contrary to the mandate of law this Court should direct him for performing such function. But it is surprising for us to see that none of the resigning members of the parliament has come forward to seek direction from us. The direction is sought by a person who has got no Constitutional right to enforce in the matter of acceptance of resignation letters because he cannot take advantage of any of the rights described under Part III of the Constitution nor could he successfully plead before us that any of his legal rights has been violated. In this writ petition his standing is identical to the standing of writ petitioner in Writ Petition No.88 of 1995. In Writ Petition No.88 of 1995 I have reviewed a large number of decisions starting from the Supreme Court of America, the Supreme Court of India, the Supreme Court of Pakistan and the Appellant Division of the Supreme Court of Bangladesh and I said that the petitioner has no locus standi to maintain the writ petition under Article 102 of the Constitution specially in view of the observation made in the Sangbadpatra Parishad case wherein it has been held that for the wording of Articles 32 and 226 of Indian Constitution which is different from wording of Article 102 of the Constitution Jurisdiction of the Indian Supreme Court under Article 226 and Article 32 is much more wider than that of ours because a limiting jurisdiction is conferred under Article 102 of the Constitution by the founding fathers of the Constitution. By resignation none of the fundamental rights guaranteed under Part-III of the Constitution of the petitioner seems to have been violated. Then what is his right. If it is not a fundamental right then it must be a legal right under an Act of the Parliament. From the statements made in the petition, the Affidavit-in-opposition, the affidavit-in-reply I am unable to bring the action before us under Article 102 of the Constitution and that being the position I am of the view that the petitioner is not a "person aggrieved" and has no substantial, direct personal interest in the matter. He may have some remote interest and for such remoteness of interest which is in common with other conscious citizens of the country he has no entitlement to proceed with the Rule before us on the ground of maintainability. Accordingly, I am of the opinion that this petition also fails on the ground of standing.

In the case of Tahir Beg vs. Kausar Ali reported in PLD 1976 (SC) 504 resignation letter of the appellant, a member of the Provincial Assembly allegedly obtained by the respondent by coercion at pistol point on 16.2.74, was placed before the Speaker who caused a Gazette Notification published on the same day about resignation of the appellant. In that case resignation of the appellant was considered by the House in a privilege motion adopted by the House on 24.5.74. So it was claimed that resignation of the appellant formed part of the internal proceeding of the House under Article 69 of the Constitution of Pakistan 1973 and Court has no jurisdiction to enquire into the matter. Md. Gul J after reviewing the decisions in the case Ahmed Syed Kirmani reported in PLD 1958 (SC) 379; Lt. Col. Farzand Ali Vs. Province of West Pakistan reported in 22 DLR (SC) 203=PLD 1970 (SC) 98 and Fazlul Quader Chowdhury vs. Md. Abdul Haque reported in 18 DLR (SC) 69=PLD 1963 SC 486 held that "Therefore, there is no merit in the second limb of the argument of the appellant's learned counsel. The question at the root is not validity of the resolution of the Provincial Assembly accepting the privilege motion on 24.5.74, but the right, title of the appellant to continue as member of the Assembly and therefore, inevitably a question relating to "composition" of the House, which the superior courts in the sub-continent have not hesitated to consider and decide in appropriate proceedings."
